Many of the same trees found in Olinder also occur in Mayfair, for example, Silk Oak, Cedar, Southern Magnolia, Coast Redwoods, Birches, Black Locust, Walnut and Olives. However, in contrast to Olinder, Mayfair has no riparian community because Silver Creek Channel has been lined with concrete and flows only intermittenly. The animal life in Mayfair is similar to the residential portions of Olinder and Campus except that Beechey Ground Squirrels and Western Meadowlarks are to be found on the vacant lots.
Northside CNRA:
The Northside area encompasses three City parks, Backesto, Empire Gardens and Fred Watson Park. Coyote Creek passes through these last two parks along the easterly side of the CNRA. The riparian (creekside) habitat and wildlife found here is similar to that described for Coyote Creek under Olinder except that the flood plain on the western side of the creek has been preserved for open space. In addition to the typical riparian animal life, Beechey Ground Squirrels are common across the open grassy area of the flood plain. Here, there are old Block Cottonwoods, Live Oaks, and Box Elders while many younger Monterey and Stone Pines have been planted more recently. Next to the new park building at the end of Jackson Street there are Trees of Heaven and Black Locusts preserved in landscaping.
Backesto Park is encircled by a peripheral row of large Sycamores with a variety of mature trees lying on the interior. On the westerly side of the Park behind the Sycamores is a row of Coast Redwoods while on the South there are several large Live Oak and Elms. Other park landscaping includes lawn and shrubery. Lying to the west of the Park at 590 North 21st Street is the so-called "Sentinel Tree" an unusually large Sycamore which has historical significance in addition to its mammoth size. Along 21st Street, as well as throughout the northside, the most common trees are Walnuts, Sycamores, Birches, Cedars, Olives, Carobs, and California Peppers. The trees and residential landscaping are similar in age to the Olinder and with the towering Washington Palms and Coast Redwoods telling of their planting long ago. Located just north of Jackson on 19th Street is a Giant Sequoia (Big Tree) which is somewhat unusual to find in San Jose although it is by no means the only one in the city.
Olinder CNRA:
As an old residential area, Olinder is abundantly stocked with mature trees and landscaping. The most common trees found in yards and along the street are Walnuts and Sycamores while examples of others which occur frequent are: California Pepper, Deodar Cedar, Coast Redwoods, Black Locust, Tree of Heaven, Sweet Gum, Tulip Tree, Pines, Birch, Loquat, Blackwood Acacia, and Carob Tree. As in other residential areas, other landscaping includes lawns, flower beds and shrubs such as Pyracantha, Roses, Juniper, Bottlebrush Ivy and the like. One of the most interesting trees is a native California-Laurel and it is found at a few locations in Olinder. The tree is frequently found in association with streams and drainages.
